title: Job 18:1–10
context: Bildad the Shuhite speaks in his second speech. He rebukes Job’s words (18:2–4) and begins a poem on the fate of the wicked, whose light goes out and who is caught in traps of his own making (18:5–10). This is a friend’s case, not the book’s verdict: the reader already knows from 1:8 and 2:3 that Job is blameless, and the LORD later says the friends have not spoken of him what is right (42:7).

verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces Bildad’s second speech. Arminian readers note from the outset that the book later says the friends did not speak rightly of God (42:7), so Bildad’s words are a case to be weighed, not the book’s verdict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise begin by noting that Bildad speaks as one of the three friends whom the LORD later rebukes (42:7). His speech is reported faithfully, but it should be read as one voice in a debate rather than as settled doctrine.

verses.text: “How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and afterwards we will speak.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad asks, “How long will you hunt for words?” Arminian readers see the friend’s impatience with Job’s complaints and a refusal to hear his anguish as anything more than wordiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the debate hardening. Bildad treats Job’s laments as empty speech, and readers in this tradition note how quickly a friend’s counsel can turn into rebuke when suffering does not fit expectations.

verses.text: Why are we counted as animals, which have become unclean in your sight?
verses.arminianNotes: “Why are we counted as animals, which have become unclean in your sight?” Arminian readers see Bildad stung by Job’s dismissal of the friends, which turns the conversation toward wounded pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see personal offense shaping Bildad’s words. The exchange shows how argument about suffering can drift into defending oneself, a pattern readers in this tradition find pastorally instructive.

verses.text: You who tear yourself in your anger, will the earth be forsaken for you? Or will the rock be removed out of its place?
verses.arminianNotes: “You who tear yourself in your anger, will the earth be forsaken for you?” Arminian readers see Bildad insisting that the moral order will not change to suit Job’s complaint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Bildad defending a fixed order of retribution. His rhetorical question assumes he already knows how God governs Job’s case, an assumption the book later calls into question.

verses.text: “Yes, the light of the wicked will be put out. The spark of his fire won’t shine.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad begins his poem: “Yes, the light of the wicked will be put out.” Arminian readers see a traditional picture of the end of the wicked, true in its place but misapplied when aimed at Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that Scripture elsewhere speaks of the downfall of the wicked, while noting that Bildad’s error lies in assuming Job’s suffering proves Job wicked. The book’s prologue (1:8) has already told readers otherwise.

verses.text: The light will be dark in his tent. His lamp above him will be put out.
verses.arminianNotes: “The light will be dark in his tent. His lamp above him will be put out.” Arminian readers see imagery of a household brought to ruin, which Bildad seems to apply pointedly to Job’s own losses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of an extinguished lamp. Bildad does not name Job, but readers in this tradition commonly hear an implied accusation in light of Job’s bereavement in chapter 1.

verses.text: The steps of his strength will be shortened. His own counsel will cast him down.
verses.arminianNotes: “The steps of his strength will be shortened. His own counsel will cast him down.” Arminian readers see Bildad’s claim that the wicked are undone by their own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the theme of self-defeating wickedness. Readers in this tradition note that such statements can be true as general patterns without proving anything about a particular sufferer.

verses.text: For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he wanders into its mesh.
verses.arminianNotes: “For he is cast into a net by his own feet.” Arminian readers see hunting imagery describing how the wicked walk into their own ruin through their chosen paths.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of entrapment. Job will later answer that it is God who has surrounded him with his net (19:6), turning Bildad’s picture in a startling direction.

verses.text: A snare will take him by the heel. A trap will catch him.
verses.arminianNotes: “A snare will take him by the heel. A trap will catch him.” Arminian readers see the piling up of trapping images to stress that the wicked cannot escape consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Bildad’s rhetoric intensifying. The repetition is meant to persuade, but readers in this tradition keep in mind that the book will judge the friends’ application of such pictures.

verses.text: A noose is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him on the path.
verses.arminianNotes: “A noose is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him on the path.” Arminian readers see hidden dangers awaiting those who walk in wickedness, a theme found in wisdom literature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize the wisdom theme of hidden snares. In Bildad’s mouth, however, it serves to warn Job as though he were the wicked man, which the narrator has not said.
